note: Scene texts of the follow-up baselines (added 2026-10-26 after the main results, not pre-registered). "premise" is what the director knows: the situation before the start anchor and the question that the scene must decide, without its answer (the question was made explicit on 2026-10-26 after the smoke tests of the director). "plot" is the plot of the original scene, summarized from the novel, as the given circumstances of CoSER-style acting (Wang et al., 2025): every character and the next-speaker predictor know it, so that condition is a reference with the ending known.

premise.pearls: Wang Lung, a rich farmer, is infatuated with Lotus, a girl of the tea house in the town, and spends his silver on presents for her. His wife O-lan, plain and silent, still keeps two small white pearls that he let her keep years ago. Wang Lung comes home over the fields to O-lan, who is washing his clothes at the pool. Wang Lung wants a present for Lotus, and O-lan has the pearls: will he ask her for them, and will she give them up? The scene must decide this.
premise.sell_the_land: Wang Lung is old and forgetful and lives on his land, which he loves above everything. His two sons, an officer of the town and a grain merchant, want money; they walk out on to his land to see which fields could be sold, and he follows them slowly with his staff. Will the sons sell part of their father's land against his will? The scene must decide this.

plot.pearls: Wang Lung comes to O-lan at the pool and roughly asks her where her pearls are. She answers timidly that she has them, that she thought she might have them set in earrings, or keep them for their younger daughter when she is wed. He scorns this, says that pearls are for fair women, and demands them. She slowly takes the small package from her bosom and gives it to him, and he laughs at the pearls in his hand. She goes back to beating his clothes on the stone, and her tears fall without her wiping them away.
plot.sell_the_land: On the land the second son tells his brother which fields they will sell and how they will divide the money, not knowing that their father has come up behind them. Wang Lung hears the words "sell the land", cries out in anger against his evil, idle sons, nearly falls and weeps. He says that a family is finished when it begins to sell its land, and holds a handful of earth. His sons hold him up and soothe him and promise again and again that the land will not be sold; but over his head they look at each other and smile.
